title: Could the Bend, Oregon, school shooter’s parents face charges? | CNN
text:
Source: CNN

It’s illegal in Oregon for anyone under 18 to possess a firearm, with a few exceptions. So how exactly did the 16-year-old who carriedout aschool shooting in Bend, Oregon, last week get access to a gun and ammunition?

That question has yet to be answered and is part of what Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz called an “active criminal investigation.”

Recent cases in Michigan and Georgia suggest either or both parents of the teenage school shooter could be held criminally liable for the killings.

In Michigan, James and Jennifer Crumbley, the parents of14-year-old school shooter Ethan Crumbley, were convicted of manslaughter and sentenced to 10 to 15 years in prison. In Georgia, Colin Gray, thefather of 14-year-old school shooter Colt Gray, was convicted of murder and sentenced to 15 years in prison.

And in a pending case in Wisconsin, thefather of a 15-year-oldschool shooter faces three felony charges for allegedly allowing his daughter access to firearms. Jeffrey Rupnow, 44, has pleaded not guilty and his trial is set for March,according to court records.

Those cases were part of a broader movement pushing the limits of who is accountable for a mass shooting. For prosecutors, the goal of bringing these cases is to ensure gun-owning parents secure their firearms and thereby prevent future school shootings.

In Oregon, the investigation has only just begun but legal experts believe the investigation will follow a similar path.

“It certainly could lead to a situation like we’ve seen recently in the last few years in Georgia and also Michigan, where parents have been charged criminally,” said Andrew McCabe, CNN senior law enforcement analyst.

Like in the Michigan and Georgia cases, investigators are likely to focus on how the Oregon school shooter obtained the firearm and what the parents knew about the potential risks to others.

“I think this investigation will head the same way,” said CNN national security analyst Juliette Kayyem. “How did he get access to guns? What did the parents know?”

In theBend school shootingat Silver Rail Elementary School, the armed 16-year-old shooter killed three children and a teacher before he was fatally shot by a student’s parent. Another child and teacher also were injured, officials said.

A pump-action shotgun was found near the suspect, who had about 44 remaining rounds of ammunition, Krantz said.

The gun had been purchased by the teen’s mother, a senior law enforcement official briefed on the investigation told CNN.

PerOregon law, it’s illegal for a juvenile to possess a firearm but there are exceptions for certain long guns if the firearm was transferred by their parent or is used temporarily for hunting or target practice.

The shooter’s parents were interviewed and were cooperative, a senior law enforcement official told CNN.

A search warrant was executed at the alleged shooter’s house on Thursday and computers and other electronics were taken,the source said. Search warrants have also been obtained to gain access to the devices and extract data, according to the source.

The suspect,Griffin J. John II, was a formerspecial needsstudent at the school, police said. His mother spoke in 2020 with CNN affiliate KTVZ about his special needs and his enrollment in a program described as serving children with “intensive behavioral and social skills challenges.”

“I think it will be great for my son to get the help that he needs from the skilled teachers that he needs to get it from,” she told the station.

The suspect’s motherspoke briefly with CNNoff camera from her balcony on Friday. She said there were no warning signs and declined to comment on how her son got access to the gun.

“I’m so sorry, I wish I could have done something. I’m sorry for their loss,” she told CNN.

The criminal cases against the Crumbleys in Michigan and Colin Gray in Georgia featured similar allegations: An unsecured firearm and inattentive parents.

In each situation, a parent purchased a gun for their teenage son as a Christmas gift and left the firearm unsecured. The parents also allegedly knew their son had mental health problems and was a threat to others but did not properly address the issues by putting him into counseling or therapy.

Prosecutors argued the parents’ actions represented “criminal negligence” – and the juries agreed.

For example, in Gray’s trial, police had visited his home a year prior to the school shooting to investigate anonline threat to shoot up a school. Colt Gray denied posting the threat and law enforcement was ultimately unable to substantiate the tip.

Colin Gray bought his son an AR-15-style rifle later that year. He testified he sometimes allowed his son to keep the rifle in his bedroom, and left otherweapons and ammolying around the house.

His defense attorney said he tried his best to help his son but simply didn’t have warning about his violent plans. But prosecutors argued he acted negligently by buying a gun and ignoring warnings of the potential risk to others.

“This was a trial about this defendant’s actions, his choices and his responsibility,” Barrow County District Attorney Brad Smith said.

In the Oregon case, there are more questions than answers at this point. How did the 16-year-old get access to the firearm and ammo? What did the parents know of their son’s mental health issues and the potential threat he posed to others? Were there warning signs ahead of time, and what did people around him do about them?

Simply buying a gun for a child is not illegal on its own, legal experts said.

“The purchase, per se, is not necessarily improper,” said Katherine Schweit, a former Chicago prosecutor and FBI special agent.

McCabe said investigators will be looking for more than just a purchase history.

“They’ll need evidence, actual proof that the parent knew that, let’s say, the minor was in a vulnerable state. And the parent, despite knowing that, basically gave the minor access to the firearm, knowing that they might be in a vulnerable position,” he said.

“Those are all hard things to prove after the fact. So we’ll have to see what comes out of the investigation.”

CNN’s John Miller, Nick Watt, Norma Galeana and Alaa Elassar contributed to this report.

CNN’s John Miller, Nick Watt, Norma Galeana and Alaa Elassar contributed to this report.
